**Short answer** | Regime | What you must prove | Where it differs from the other regime | Documentation you should keep | |--------|---------------------|---------------------------------------|--------------------------------| | **UK (post‑Brexit)** | • The processing of employee HR records is lawful under Article 6(1)(b) or (c) and Article 9(2)(i).
• Because Germany is an EU member state, the UK treats it as a *third country* after Brexit. Therefore you must use **adequate safeguards** – most commonly Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) or Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs). | • The UK has no “adequacy” decision for Germany; the transfer is governed by UK law, not EU adequacy.
• The UK Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has issued post‑Schrems II guidance that SCCs must be supplemented with a *risk assessment* and evidence that the recipient country provides an “adequate” level of protection. | • DPIA (or risk assessment).
• Transfer documentation showing choice of safeguard, mapping of data flows, and justification for SCCs.
• Processor agreement **with SCCs appended**.
• Evidence of lawful basis (policy statements, employee consent where used).
• Records of any employee rights requests and how they were handled. | | **EU (GDPR)** | • The processing is lawful under Article 6(1)(b)/(c) and Article 9(2)(i).
• Because the data leave a *non‑EU* country (the UK), you must use an “adequate” safeguard – SCCs or BCRs. | • The EU treats Germany as part of the EU, so there is no adequacy decision for the destination; the transfer is governed by GDPR Article 44–50.
• The EU Data Protection Authorities (DPAs) have been scrutinising SCCs after *Schrems II* and may require additional evidence that the UK provides an adequate level of protection. | • DPIA (or risk assessment).
• Transfer documentation showing choice of safeguard, mapping, and justification for SCCs.
• Processor agreement **with SCCs appended**.
• Evidence of lawful basis.
• Records of employee rights requests. | --- ## 1. UK regime (post‑Brexit) ### 1.1 Lawful basis for processing HR records | Article | Basis | Why it applies to employee data | |---------|-------|---------------------------------| | **UK GDPR Art 6(1)(b)** | Necessary for the performance of a contract | Employment contracts require HR data (pay, benefits, leave). | | **UK GDPR Art 6(1)(c)** | Compliance with a legal obligation | Employers must keep records for tax, statutory reporting, etc. | | **UK GDPR Art 9(2)(i)** | Processing of special‑category data necessary for employment | HR data often contain health or biometric information; this article permits processing if it is essential for the contract. | > **Assumption**: All 340 employees’ records are processed solely for legitimate employment purposes (contract performance and legal compliance). > **Training‑cutoff note**: “As of my training data up to 2024‑06, these provisions remain unchanged.” ### 1.2 Transfer mechanism - **Adequacy decision?** No – Germany is an EU member state; the UK no longer has an adequacy decision for it after Brexit. - **Safeguards required**: - **Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs)** – the most common, provided by the European Commission and adapted for UK use. - **Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs)** – possible if you operate a group of companies; unlikely for a single processor. - **Additional requirements after Schrems II**: - The ICO requires that you conduct a *risk assessment* to confirm that the recipient country offers an adequate level of protection, even when SCCs are used. - You must document how the German processor implements technical and organisational measures (e.g., ISO 27001 certification, encryption). ### 1.3 Documentation | Item | Purpose | Where it sits in your records | |------|---------|------------------------------| | **Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)** or risk assessment | Demonstrates that the transfer is low‑risk or mitigated | File under “Transfer Risk Assessments” | | **Mapping of data flows** (source, destination, purpose) | Shows what data are moved and why | Part of DPIA | | **Processor agreement with SCCs appended** | Legal contract binding processor to UK GDPR obligations | Under “Contracts – Processor Agreements” | | **Evidence of lawful basis** (policy statements, employee consent where used) | Shows compliance with Article 6/9 | In the HR policy archive | | **Records of data subject rights requests** (access, rectification, erasure) | Demonstrates that you can honour rights across borders | Under “Data Subject Rights” | > **Note**: The processor agreement must be updated to include the SCCs *in full*, not just a reference. The UK version of the SCCs is slightly different from the EU version (e.g., wording about “third‑country” and “adequate protection”), so use the UK‑adapted clauses. --- ## 2. EU regime (GDPR) ### 2.1 Lawful basis for processing HR records | Article | Basis | Why it applies | |---------|-------|----------------| | **Art 6(1)(b)** | Contract performance | Same as in UK GDPR. | | **Art 6(1)(c)** | Legal obligation | EU law requires employers to keep certain data (e.g., for tax, social security). | | **Art 9(2)(i)** | Special categories necessary for employment | HR data often include health or biometric information; this article permits processing. | > **Assumption**: The same lawful basis applies in the EU as in the UK because the legal nature of employment is identical. ### 2.2 Transfer mechanism - **Adequacy decision?** No – the transfer is from a *non‑EU* country (UK) to an EU member state (Germany). - **Safeguards required**: - **SCCs** – the European Commission’s SCCs are valid for transfers from the UK after Brexit, provided you use the UK‑adapted version. - **BCRs** – possible but rarely used by a single processor. - **Post‑Schrems II scrutiny**: EU DPAs have been reviewing whether SCCs still provide adequate protection when data leave the UK. They may require additional evidence that the UK offers an “adequate” level of protection (e.g., through a *risk assessment* or *data transfer impact assessment*). ### 2.3 Documentation | Item | Purpose | Where it sits | |------|---------|---------------| | **DPIA / risk assessment** | Shows that the transfer is low‑risk or mitigated | Under “Transfer Risk Assessments” | | **Mapping of data flows** | Clarifies what data are moved and why | Part of DPIA | | **Processor agreement with SCCs appended** | Binds processor to GDPR obligations | Under “Contracts – Processor Agreements” | | **Evidence of lawful basis** (policy statements, employee consent) | Demonstrates compliance with Article 6/9 | In HR policy archive | | **Records of data subject rights requests** | Shows ability to honour rights across borders | Under “Data Subject Rights” | > **Note**: The EU SCCs contain a clause that the transfer must be “necessary for the performance of a contract or for compliance with a legal obligation.” This aligns with the UK basis, but you must ensure the wording matches the UK version. --- ## 3. Divergences between the regimes | Issue | UK perspective | EU perspective | |-------|----------------|----------------| | **Adequacy status** | Germany is a *third country*; no adequacy decision for the UK. | Germany is inside the EU; the transfer is from a non‑EU to an EU state, so no adequacy decision for the destination. | | **Regulatory authority** | ICO (UK) – focuses on whether SCCs are supplemented with a risk assessment and whether the UK offers adequate protection. | EU DPAs – focus on whether SCCs meet GDPR Article 46 requirements; they may require additional evidence of UK protection levels after Schrems II. | | **Contractual wording** | Use the *UK‑adapted* SCCs (different clauses about “third country” and “adequate protection”). | Use the *EU‑adapted* SCCs (different clauses about “adequacy decision” and “public authority”). | | **Enforcement emphasis** | ICO has issued guidance that if you rely on SCCs, you must demonstrate that the UK offers an adequate level of protection; failure to do so may lead to enforcement action. | EU DPAs have been more aggressive post‑Schrems II in scrutinising SCCs and may require additional safeguards or even block transfers if they deem them insufficient. | > **What would change your conclusion?** > • If the UK were granted an adequacy decision for Germany (unlikely). > • If the EU DPAs decided that the UK no longer provides adequate protection, you might need to adopt BCRs or obtain explicit employee consent. > • If the processor in Germany fails to implement the required technical measures (e.g., encryption), both regulators could enforce corrective action. --- ## 4. Documentation checklist | Document | Who prepares it | Where to store it | |----------|-----------------|-------------------| | **Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)** or risk assessment for the transfer | Data protection officer (DPO) + IT & HR | “Transfer Risk Assessments” folder, version‑controlled | | **Mapping of data flows** (source → destination, purpose, retention period) | DPO + HR | Part of DPIA | | **Processor agreement with SCCs appended** | Legal team + processor’s legal counsel | “Contracts – Processor Agreements” | | **Evidence of lawful basis** (policy statements, employee consent forms if used) | HR & Legal | “HR Policies” archive | | **Records of data subject rights requests** (access, rectification, erasure) | DPO / Data Subject Rights team | “Data Subject Rights” log | | **Audit logs and technical measures evidence** (e.g., ISO 27001 certificate, encryption keys) | IT & Security | “Security & Compliance” repository | | **Transfer documentation** (justification for SCCs, risk assessment summary) | DPO | “Transfer Documentation” folder | > **Assumption**: The processor agreement already exists but does not contain the UK‑adapted SCCs; you will need to add them. > **Training‑cutoff note**: “As of my training data up to 2024‑06, the above documents are considered best practice and align with ICO and EU DPA guidance.” --- ## 5. Enforcement position – actively developing | Regime | Current enforcement stance (as of 2024‑06) | What you should monitor | |--------|-------------------------------------------|--------------------------| | **UK (ICO)** | The ICO has issued “Cross‑border data transfer guidance” post‑Schrems II, emphasizing the need for a *risk assessment* and evidence that the UK offers adequate protection. They have started to issue enforcement notices against companies that rely on SCCs without proper risk mitigation. | ICO’s Enforcement Tracker; any updates on adequacy decisions or new guidance on “adequate protection” | | **EU (DPAs)** | Several DPAs (e.g., France, Germany) have issued warnings about the use of UK SCCs after Schrems II and are demanding additional safeguards or blocking transfers if they deem them insufficient. The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) has not yet issued a definitive ruling but is monitoring the situation closely. | EDPB opinions; national DPA enforcement actions; any new EU adequacy decisions involving the UK | | **Cross‑border** | Both regulators are increasingly aligning on the requirement that *adequate protection* must be demonstrable, even when SCCs are used. Non‑compliance can lead to fines up to 4 % of global turnover (EU) or £17.5 m (UK). | Regulatory press releases; updates from the ICO and EU DPAs; industry newsletters | > **What would change your conclusion?** > • If a new EU adequacy decision were issued for the UK, you could rely on that instead of SCCs. > • If either regulator introduced a “transparency requirement” (e.g., mandatory public register of transfers), you would need to update your documentation accordingly. --- ### Bottom line 1. **UK**: Use the UK‑adapted SCCs, supplement them with a DPIA/risk assessment, and keep detailed records of lawful basis and employee rights. 2. **EU**: Use the EU‑adapted SCCs (or BCRs), also backed by a DPIA/risk assessment, and maintain the same set of documentation. 3. **Divergence**: The main difference is in the *legal wording* of the SCCs and the regulatory authority that will enforce them. 4. **Documentation**: Prepare a DPIA, data‑flow map, processor agreement with SCCs appended, evidence of lawful basis, employee consent records (if any), rights‑request logs, and technical safeguards evidence. By following this checklist you’ll satisfy both UK and EU requirements and be prepared for the evolving enforcement landscape.
